prompts.L3:

- The speaker understands John’s distress because his wife also left during the night to avoid being sold south.
- The speaker is hurt that John mocked his desire to leave, even after they had spent five years together.
- He has secured a small but clean room in Philadelphia where they can build a life and possibly raise children.
- He imagines creating a home where both of them can live freely, beyond the shadow of the lash.
- He gives John a new suit, urging him to walk proudly in clothes meant for a free man.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

An enslaved speaker confronts John about his wife’s impending sale and urges him to escape with her to Philadelphia, imagining a clean room, children, and a shared life beyond slavery. By giving John an unworn suit as “free man’s clothes,” she transforms escape into a vision of dignity, family, and freedom from the lash’s shadow.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: john lord knows

outputs.L1:
John, Lord knows you’re still vexed. Reckon I am too. If my wife stole off during the sleepy night—God and the Devil the only souls awake at that hour—even if I knew she was about to be sold South, even if I knew she was leaving...

And you did know. You were so troubled whenever I spoke of leaving. Called me a fool. Called me Cudjo. Five years with you, John, and your wife about to be sold away just because you’re free—and still, that don’t worry you none. You laugh. Don’t know if I’d miss your laugh if I were in the South, though.

Thank you, Jesus, I got a room in Philadelphia, John. Ain’t big, but it’s clean. Enough room for us—and some children too. Your baby, I ain’t too old just yet. Just around thirty-one, I think.

Let’s make us a home, John. One where we’re both free—free from the lash’s shadow, free like the Lord meant.

Got this suit for you, John. Ain’t nobody worn these clothes before. Walk proud in these clothes. These are a free man’s clothes.
outputs.L2:
John, heaven knows you’re still angry—and I suppose I am as well. If my wife slipped away in the dead of night, when only God, the devil, and wandering spirits are awake, I’d be upset too, even if I knew she was escaping because she was about to be sold South. But you knew she planned to leave, and still you became so distressed whenever I spoke of leaving. Call me foolish. Call me Cudjo. I’ve spent five years with you, John.

Your wife is about to be taken away and sold simply because you’re free, yet you act as though it doesn’t trouble you. You even laugh. Though I wonder whether I’d miss that laugh if I were down South.

Thank Jesus, I have a place in Philadelphia. It isn’t large, but it’s clean and has enough space for us—and for a few children as well. Your baby, John. I’m not too old yet; I believe I’m only around thirty-one. We could build a life together there, in a home where both of us are free—beyond even the shadow of the whip, free in the way the Lord intended.

I brought you this suit, John. No one has ever worn it before. Stand tall when you put it on. These are the clothes of a free man.
outputs.L3:
The speaker understands John’s distress more deeply than John may realize. His own wife once slipped away in the night rather than risk being sold south, leaving him with the same pain of sudden separation and loss. For that reason, he is especially hurt that John mocked his desire to leave, despite the five years they have spent together and the bond they have formed.

Still, the speaker offers John the possibility of a new beginning. He has secured a small but clean room in Philadelphia, a place where they can build a life and perhaps one day raise children. He imagines creating a true home there, where they can live freely and no longer exist under the threat of the overseer’s lash. As a symbol of that freedom, he gives John a new suit and urges him to wear it proudly—to stand tall in clothes made not for an enslaved man, but for a free one.
outputs.L4:
John, they mean to sell your wife.

I heard it this morning, though no one thought I was listening. The papers are nearly drawn, and the buyer may come before the week is out. Once she is taken away, there will be no promise that you will ever learn where she has gone. You know how it happens: a wagon leaves the yard, the road swallows it, and a family is broken as easily as a stick beneath a boot.

You must not let that happen. Go to her tonight. Tell her to gather only what she can carry. When the house is quiet and the moon has gone down, take the north road and do not turn back. There are people who will help you if you reach them, people who know the hidden paths and the safe doors. Keep moving until you come to Philadelphia.

Think of it, John. In Philadelphia you might have a room of your own—a small room, perhaps, but clean, with a bed no one can order you out of and a door you may close against the world. Your wife could wake beside you without fearing that the day would tear her away. You could work for wages and bring the money home in your own hands. In time, there might be children. They would bear your name. No one would stand over them counting their value or threatening to sell them south. They could grow up knowing you as their father, not as a man forced to bow whenever another man spoke.

I know the road is dangerous. I know what they will do if they catch you. The lash has cast its shadow across every choice we have ever made. But if you remain here, that shadow will fall over all the years to come. Your wife will be gone, and you will spend your life wondering where she sleeps, whether she is hungry, whether she still calls for you.

So I have brought you something.

The suit has never been worn. I kept it folded carefully, away from dust and damp. Put it on when you leave. These are not a servant’s clothes, nor clothes chosen by a master to mark what he thinks you are. They are a free man’s clothes. Wear them and remember that freedom is more than crossing a boundary. It is standing upright. It is choosing where to go, whom to love, and what kind of life to build.

Take the suit, John. Take your wife’s hand. Go north, and do not stop until the lash’s shadow can no longer reach you.
outputs.L5:
### John Lord Knows

John Lord knows that life rarely follows a perfect plan. Every choice brings new possibilities, and every challenge offers a lesson. While others may rush toward quick answers, John prefers to pause, observe, and trust his experience.

He understands that wisdom is not about knowing everything—it is about remaining curious, listening carefully, and learning from mistakes. John Lord knows that patience, honesty, and determination can turn even difficult moments into opportunities for growth.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a raw, historically grounded monologue in dialect from an enslaved man named Cudjo to his free friend John, urging him to escape to Philadelphia before John’s wife is sold South.
counterfactuals.output:
“John, look at me. Don’t turn your face off like you ain’t heard. You know what that trader’s wagon mean. You heard them chains dragged out the storehouse. By Saturday they mean to sell your Ruth—sell her down through Richmond, maybe farther, where the cotton eat folks alive. Once they put her in that coffle, you ain’t likely to see her no more in this world.

“You free by paper, John, but what kind of freedom stand still while a man take his wife? That paper can’t comfort you when her side of the bed gone cold.

“Go tonight. Don’t wait for law, ’cause law was writ for them that own the courthouse. Get Ruth away before they lock her in the jail. Make for Philadelphia. There’s colored folks there, free people with houses and churches, and white Quakers too, some that won’t ask no price before they help. Find the Vigilance men. Keep your freedom paper dry, but don’t trust it to save Ruth. Her safety got to come first.

“I can’t go with you. Master count me every morning same as he count his mules. But I can stand here one more day and lie. I can say I seen nothing. I can point a man the wrong road. That little piece of help still mine to give.

“John, they sell us by waiting. They say tomorrow, next week, after harvest—then somebody’s child gone, somebody’s woman gone South, and all that’s left is a name folks scared to speak. Don’t let Ruth turn into a name.

“Take her hand. Leave the skillet, leave the bedstead, leave every blessed thing that can be bought again. Philadelphia ain’t heaven. Slave catchers walk there too, and freedom got enemies even on free soil. But there’s people there who’ll call Ruth a woman, not property. That’s more mercy than she’ll find in that trader’s wagon.

“Go now, brother. Be afraid on the road if you got to—but don’t be afraid here till it’s too late.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a stream-of-consciousness speech set during American slavery in which a man offers John a clean room, the hope of children and a new home, and an unworn suit he calls “free man’s clothes.”
counterfactuals.output:
“John, listen—don’t look toward the yard, don’t look where they can see your wanting. I have a room for you, clean walls, a bed raised off the floor, a window facing east so the sun comes before anybody’s orders. Your own basin. Your own door. Think of that, John: a door no man can open merely because he owns the key.

And there may be children yet. Yours—not names entered beside the price of a mule, not little hands carried south to settle another man’s debt. Children who wake beneath your roof and call no one master. A new home, John. Not heaven; I won’t lie and call it heaven. There’ll be cold, work, fear, people watching. But the work will have your name on it, and the fear won’t wear a whip.

I brought you a suit. Never worn. Black wool, brass buttons, shirt white as Sunday linen. Free man’s clothes, I call them. Though cloth cannot free a body, I know that. A coat can’t tear up a ledger, trousers can’t stop a rider, and shoes don’t promise the road will be kind. Still, put them on. Feel how they were cut for a man standing straight.

Come before dawn. Come while the house is dreaming it owns tomorrow. Leave the old shirt folded by the pallet if you wish, like a skin you have stepped out of. Or burn it. Or carry it, so you never forget.

But come, John. The room is waiting. The suit is waiting. Somewhere beyond this night, children who do not yet exist are waiting to bear your name.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an emotionally intense theatrical monologue where Cudjo confronts John about his wife fleeing at night to avoid being sold, then gives John a new suit and tells him to walk proudly as a free man.
counterfactuals.output:
*[Night. CUDJO stands before JOHN, holding a folded suit. His voice begins low, trembling with contained fury.]*

**CUDJO:**

John—look at me.

Your wife did not run because she had forgotten you. She did not slip into that black night because she was faithless, or foolish, or unafraid. She ran because morning was coming, and with morning came the hands that would weigh her like cotton, examine her teeth like livestock, and put a price upon the heart that loved you.

She ran because they meant to sell her.

Do you hear me, John? Sell her laughter. Sell her labor. Sell every tomorrow she had promised you. Send her down some road where your voice could never reach her again.

So she chose the darkness. Bare feet on cold ground. Thorns cutting her skin. Every snapping branch sounding like a gun behind her. She carried no lantern—only terror, and the memory of your face.

Do not curse her for going.

Curse the world that made staying more terrible than flight.

*[He thrusts the folded suit toward JOHN, then softens.]*

Take this.

No—do not shrink from it. Put it on.

These sleeves were not made for a man in chains. This coat does not belong bowed over a field. These buttons are not another master’s mark. They are yours.

Tonight, you will stand straight.

You will lift your head even if sorrow hangs from it like iron. You will walk through that door not as property, not as a number scratched beside a price, not as a man waiting for permission to breathe.

You will walk as a free man.

And if the world stares, let it stare. If it trembles to see you proud, let it tremble. Every step you take will say what they tried to beat out of us:

*I belong to no one.*

Walk for your wife, wherever the night carried her. Walk so that, somehow, she may feel the earth answer beneath your feet.

Go on, John.

Put on the suit.

Then walk proudly enough for both of you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a fragmented, period-style soliloquy about friendship, slavery, escape, marriage, and freedom, ending with the line “these is free man’s clothes.”
counterfactuals.output:
Friend—aye, the word warms and wounds alike. A hand at midnight. A crust divided. A whisper through the boards: *Run.*

Slavery hath no sleep. It keeps the ledger open, counts the breath, brands even a man’s dreaming as theft. Yet the river runs unowned. The north star draws no master’s wage. Beyond the field, beyond the dogs and lanterns—there lies a road made only by the taking of it.

And marriage—sweet covenant, cruelly broken at another’s pleasure. My wife, my heart: sold south, they said, as though love were livestock. Still I carry her name beneath my tongue. Freedom without her is a door opening upon an empty room.

But my friend gave me his coat. “Go,” says he. “Live enough for both.”

So I go—ragged, hunted, husband still, slave no longer. Let the old garments lie in the mud with the chains.

these is free man’s clothes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
